utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 17th of September, 2009. I would like to greet our witness, the professor, who is Praljak Defence witness; Defence counsel, Mr. Scott; his associates, as well as all of the people assisting us in the courtroom. The Trial Chamber will, first of all, hand down a decision on time allocation for Alojz Arbutina, the testimony of that witness. The witness, Alojz Arbutina, should testify pursuant to 92 ter before this Trial Chamber on Tuesday, the 22nd of September, 2009. The Trial Chamber grants the Praljak Defence one hour to conduct its examination-in-chief and perhaps also a redirect. In light of specific requests and topics addressed by the witness, in line with Guide-line number 7 of the decision on the adoption of Guide-line 4, the presentation of Defence evidence of the 24th of October, 2008, to grant the Prosecution one hour, and one hour to the other Defence teams. As far as Arbutina is concerned, the Praljak Defence will have one hour, the other Defence teams will have 30 minutes, and the Prosecutor will have one hour. As far as Arbutina is concerned, well, that is it, but we will also hand down a decision for the other witness Arbutina [as interpreted]. Looking at the schedule for next week, we will hear Arbutina to begin with. Then we will hear Miroslav Crnkovic, who will come second, and Zvonimir Skender will be third. The Trial Chamber is, therefore, asking the Praljak Defence to organise itself in such a way that if we were to finish Mr. Arbutina in the afternoon of the 22nd of September, then we can then hear the second witness straight away, Crnkovic on the Tuesday. And if we were to finish Crnkovic on the Wednesday, we should be able to hear Mr. Skender straight after that. So it is important that the Praljak Defence team organise itself in such a way that the witnesses can all be heard in quick succession. Theoretically, there is one hour, but the Prosecutor may decide not to use all of its time. The Defence team may decide not to put any additional questions in that case. We may have a gap between witnesses. That said, Mr. Skender is scheduled for Thursday. There's a fair chance that his testimony, as the schedule provides, continues on the -- on Monday, the 28th of September. So we have reason to expect him to stay over the weekend. Mr. Kovacic, do as best you can to make sure that there are no gaps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the decision was handed down on the 24th of April, 2008, and not the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, for your guidance, I would like to inform you that we always plan our work in such a way that we try to have witnesses appear here one after another. Of course, we have problems with travel, but other sections of this Tribunal deal with that. One of the principles is that witnesses should not be brought here too early because it causes them problems, being here. On the other hand, they should not be brought here too late because then we don't have enough time for our proofing session. So I'm just trying to note that there are many elements that we have to take into account. Sometimes it's impossible to envisage how long it would take, but that's the least of our problems. And we will endeavour, definitely, to try and have witnesses appear without any breaks between their testimonies, but I cannot, of course, offer you any firm guarantees because there are problems here. But this is our goal, to have them appear here continuously so that we don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do as best you can. Mr. Scott, you have the floor. Let me remind you that you have 50 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning each of Your Honours. Good morning to all counsel and all those in the courtroom and around the courtroom. And good morning, Mr. Jurcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, at the risk of going backward just for a couple of minutes, as I reviewed my notes for this final session, in light of a number of things that have been said about the Jasenovac camp, I just wanted to come back to a couple of documents that I skipped over yesterday because of time. Could you please look at Exhibit 10527, which I believe will be in the third binder. If we could have the usher -- oh, I think he has it. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 10527 in binder number 3. Sir, this is a news article from the "Toronto Star," dated the 18th of July, 1991, concerning, among other things, the Jasenovac camp. And, again, in light of some of the things that were said in the last several days, I'd like to touch on a couple of points here. The first -- the first article says: "Jasenovac is a name as dreadful in history as Dachau, Buchenwald, or Auschwitz, and what happened at this former death camp lies at the heart of a blood-feud between Serbs and Croats that threatens to destroy Yugoslavia. Serbs and Croats disagree on almost everything about this evil place, who died there, and why, and whether it could happen again. "During World War II, Croatia's fascist Ustasha regime slaughtered thousands of people here, primarily with hammers and knives. Most of the victims were Jews, gypsies, and Serbs. "In the final month of the war, the Ustasha tried to destroy the evidence. Guards burned their archives, dynamited the barracks, and massacred almost all the starving inmates." And let me pause there. If I understood you correctly, whatever other differences we might have on the topic, sir, I believe I heard you say, in response to questions from Ms. Alaburic, that you agree that what happened at Jasenovac was truly a set of horrific crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is undoubted, but we discussed this topic at length yesterday, and you tried to disqualify me very harshly, as a human being and as a professional, and about -- on the topic of Jasenovac, but without quoting a single sentence that I produced. I wrote several thousands of pages in books, various scientific papers, and I made public speeches, so I would like you to look at what I publicly stated very clearly regarding my position on Jasenovac. And you have thousands of pages that are accessible to you. If nowhere else, you can access them at my web site, which I know that you're aware of. In the public life in Croatia, to prevent public disqualifications of my person in various ways, all my media appearances, books, papers, and so on, I put them on the web site so that they are publicly accessible, and new stuff is added every day. I understand your interest -- your job to try to impeach me as a human being, well, and I have good nerves, I am tough in the fibre, and I accept to suffer that, although this will be to my detriment, and I do not have any way to obtain satisfaction. But, please, I beg you to use articles that I produced, my words, not this article which I see here for the first time. I stated thousands of times that the Ustasha regime was a totalitarian regime, that it was responsible for all of its crimes, and in layperson's terms, if you want, it's an embarrassment, it's a shame for the Croatian people, like all the rest of the totalitarian history of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I'm -- again, we only have 50 minutes or less now, so I appreciate that. The numbers that people have talked about, in terms of the number of people who died or were killed at the camp, ranged from anywhere from -- well, as large as in the hundreds of thousands, I think some numbers are even as high as 500.000 or 600.000. But be that as it may, and again, sir, my point is not to get too heavily into this further this morning, but isn't it true that even on a very conservative basis, even a most conservative number, is that somewhere between 85.000 to 100.000 people, prisoners, were killed at Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I say, and I stress again, and this is one of the key arguments in my Master's thesis, is that any number presented about Jasenovac is not scientifically founded, including the smallest number, which is astonishing, and that is that 55 people -- only 55 people were killed there. That's one of the claims. To the claim -- back to the claim of 4.400.000 [as interpreted], and in between those two figures, lots of numbers were presented in the history of Yugoslavia and Croatia, but no figure -- well, you've asked me. I'm sorry. You asked me, and I claim that no figure -- please, listen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No figure has a scientific verification, and it is, in fact, manipulation with the victims of the war, and it is my scientific position that you have to determine the number of victims, but these efforts are hampered, including by the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia, that has archives about it. And it's not true that the archives have been destroyed. And the partisan forces entered the camp the first, and they took over the documents. I wrote about that, and those documents are now in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, just one correction of the transcript. I think it's going to be important. At page 6, line 23 and 24, the witness said 1.400.000 victims as the highest number, and it says 4 million. So we don't want to have any confusion there. It's 1 million.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. You talk when you are asked. Two lines above, line 22, it says that 55 people -- only 55 people were killed there. Is that what you say, 55, five times eleven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe the witness answers. It's a matter of the record, and then you get the floor. Did you say 55?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We seem to be thinking alike. This figure, 55, and a million and 400.000, it comes from the Yugoslav Communist sources, but it's an astonishing number, 55. It is listed in the Survey Committee of the Yugoslav system. And the million and 400.000, it's again a Yugoslav source. And you have thousands of figures in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure that the record is correct. That's all. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that he wasn't suggesting that his figure is 55. It was very clear, from what I was able to hear. But the gentleman needs to slow down, and I suggest he drink some water and breathe a little bit, so that we can get an accurate record and we don't have these misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to go back to my pending question, and I didn't -- at your request, I didn't cut you off, but let me go back to the actual question I put to you. And, again, it's -- this part of it, at least, is a yes-or-no answer. You've indicated there's a wide range of numbers that have been thrown about. I'm asking you, and to assist the Judges, that even if we use what are considered some of the most conservative numbers, wouldn't you agree that at least somewhere between 85.000 to 100.000 people were killed at Jasenovac? Isn't that even a conservative -- at least even a conservative number?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with this figure or any other figure unless there is a scientific foundation. And Jasenovac was a criminal camp, regardless of how many people were killed there. People were tortured there, they were stripped of their rights, they had to do hard labour, and that's the basis of the problem. And now as for the number of victims, well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go, please, to the next exhibit. It should be very easy to find. It should be the next one, P10528, also an article from the "Toronto Star," dated the 2nd of August, 1991. Sir, at the -- and for those in the courtroom, if you look at the bottom, towards the end of the article -- well, not the end of the article, excuse me. At the bottom of the first page in English, the paragraph starting with the words: "Tudjman." And, sir, if you'll -- if nothing else, if you would listen, please, to the translation: "Tudjman was under increasing pressure from Croat extremists angry at the loss of lives and territory and eager to embark on a more aggressive military strategy. The roots of Tudjman's dilemma, Western envoys say, stretch back to his accession to power after an election campaign marked by nationalist symbolism. For the 600.000 ethnic Serbs living in Croatia, between 11 and 12 per cent of the population, it revived dark memories of the last nationalist government in Zagreb, a puppet fascist regime installed by the Nazis in World War II. Under cover of the war, Croat forces killed tens of thousands of ethnic Serbs, Jews, and gypsies, many of them in the notorious Jasenovac concentration camp. The numbers were enormous, said a Western diplomat. People argue about it, but the historical fact is it was in the hundreds of thousands. 'Perhaps Tudjman's biggest mistake, and it's really awful, is that his government has never admitted the full scale of the killing. Essentially, it's like denial of the Holocaust.'" And you knew that to be true, didn't you, sir? You knew that to be controversial, and as you said in your testimony at the Sakic trial, where one of the commanders of Jasenovac went on trial and where you appeared as a Defence witness, you said in your testimony that it was Tudjman, himself, who first talked about the "Jasenovac myth"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding the wording of the question, which might confuse the witness, in the criminal procedure -- under the criminal procedural law in Croatia, we don't have a Defence witness, Prosecution witness, or a Court witness. The only thing that exists is a witness. According to our law, the Court calls all witnesses, and experts are appointed by the Court. The procedure is particularly different when it comes to expert testimony. The Court selects the experts from a list of experts certified by County Courts, and Trial Chambers can also call other expert witnesses if there are no appropriate experts on the list. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What, then? You are telling us about the law of your country, which is interesting, but I think it's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I also do not quite see the relevance of this issue with regard to the question of Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't see it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There must be some misunderstanding. Then I will speak in English. Probably there is some mistake. The Prosecutor said -- the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With counsel's permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's hear out Mr. Kovacic, and then you respond; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, for Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So we have agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I want to avoid confusion in a witness understanding of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. The Defence witness is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Judge Trechsel, I apologise for interrupting, but I was just hoping that ultimately -- just -- I don't -- that's not -- you're exactly right, that's not my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, whatever kind of a witness you were, when you testified in that trial, the question I put to you and the crux of the question was, and given your testimony about the Jasenovac camp in that trial, you mentioned, as part of your testimony, in fact, that it was Franjo Tudjman who was the first one who started dismissing Jasenovac and talking about the Jasenovac myth. And that's the question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, and I even quoted, because you opened the document and you could see that in 1962, when Franjo Tudjman was not researching that Serbian member of the Academy --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to go back to 1962. When you testified at the trial of Mr. Sakic, did you not tell the Court -- did it not come out as part of your testimony that President Tudjman was one of the first, if not the first, to question -- to draw into question -- to talk about the Jasenovac myth? That's my question to you. Yes or no? You either gave that testimony or you didn't, and you don't need to tell me about 1962. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was one of the first to deal with this in a systematic manner while he was the head of the Institute for the History of the Working People. I said he was one of the first. It is very difficult to say who was the first, but I'm sure that the person I mentioned yesterday said this before him, and it's a member of the Academy of Sciences, Sava Bogdanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can go back to your report and spend a few more minutes on that, another section of your report concerns the destruction of the Old Bridge, and we already know that you've told us that you wrote a preface to Mr. Praljak's book on that topic. And I just want to confirm, sir, you have no first-hand knowledge of any events surrounding the destruction of the Old Bridge. Obviously, I take it, you were not there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have no expertise in artillery or military weapons, you have no expertise in explosives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have all the trust in the expert report done by the experts who did it. I have nothing else to do but to trust the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, exactly, exactly. You had nothing else to do except to lift -- completely lift the work done by Mr. Praljak and other people retained by Mr. Praljak and put it in your report. That's exactly my point, sir. I'm just trying to understand. Did you say that you were somehow providing the Judges with some sort of added evidentiary value by simply taking other people's work and putting it into your report? I don't understand -- what's the value of that? I know we have this concept of a value-added tax. What added value did you give to this, other than lifting Mr. Praljak's work and after -- and these other experts and just simply dropping that in your report? What's the point, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book, how the Old Bridge was destroyed, contains a number of various documents, contemporaneous documents, including an expert report and there were some original documents that I saw for the first time, and that compendium of documents provides a very comprehensive and systematic overview of the documents coming from various sources, from all sides, testifying in a very compelling manner that the destruction of the Old Bridge, and I think it is contained in my preface, is an open question, who did it and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the time. Let me give you one specific example. It can be found at page 123 and 124 of your report. And in that section, you say, in connection with footnote 422 -- I'm not going to -- let me just put it to you, and again, sir, if you'll listen, please. If I misread something, I'm sure I'll be corrected. On page 123 and 124 of your English report --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What footnote number?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have footnotes numbered 300 and something, so which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 422, sir, footnote 422.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the page number? Did you say "122"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it's page 123, carrying over in the English version, at least, from 123 to 124. Sir, my time is limited, and I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me help you. 147 is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 147, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that section, you say, and I'm just picking one example because we don't have time to do more, but you say: "Even they, themselves, believed in the stereotype to such an extent that the president of the Republic of Croatia," which is obviously a reference to Franjo Tudjman, "that the president of the Republic of Croatia refused to see General Praljak, who wanted to acquaint him with the facts." Now, where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a document published in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which book?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Old Bridge," the one we're discussing here, how the Old Bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't write it. He just collected the documents, and I edited or set up the book. It's a document which at that time -- well, when Franjo Tudjman refused to receive Praljak, he sent him a letter, and that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for a second, as one of my colleagues says.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... questioning, that it said -- somebody said this, but it didn't -- if that, in fact, happened, if President Tudjman refused to see Slobodan Praljak because of the issues concerning the Old Bridge, you weren't there when it happened, and I just want you to tell the Judges, very specifically: When you put this in your report, when you said -- make this statement in your report, what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absurd, if I may be allowed to say so, because nobody here in the courtroom was in the various situations, and yet we discuss them. And I'm talking about a clear document which -- it's a document. You can, of course, challenge its authenticity and so on, credibility, but you have the document in the book and you have had enough time to test its credibility. If you doubt the veracity of the documents I use, then be specific and tell us on what grounds you're saying that it's not an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... book, 422, and 422 says "Ibid," and you go back to footnote 420 -- the previous footnote, 421, and you're referring to Slobodan Praljak's book; correct? It's not so difficult.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am referring to documents, because it's a book of documents, and I've said that a number of times and emphasised it yesterday and today, and I don't know why you're wasting your valuable time, because I repeated this several times that it is just a book of documents from different sources and origins. There's no view by Praljak when the book was written. It's just a collection of documents of all kinds, including expert reports, contemporaneous documents, comments, media articles, and including criticisms and attacks on the -- on Mr. Praljak and the Croatians for having destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, I want to move forward, then, to another issue in your report. You do seem to confirm, sir, and I'm referring in particular now to pages 69 to 75, at least in the English version, of your report, where you talk about the various declarations and establishment of entities, assemblies, by the Bosnian Serbs. And your report makes it very clear, sir, that you considered and conclude and state that these various Serb declarations and assemblies were illegal, undermine the Bosnian-Herzegovinian --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might be allowed to find that part in the document, and the document as well, because I wasn't given the Croatian page. I can't look for the document and listen to what the Prosecutor is saying at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I would appreciate it very much. And as I said, if you'll just -- this is your report. I assume you're very familiar with it. I would appreciate if you can just -- if I misrepresent something to you, sir, I'm sure that one of the lawyers on the other side are going to jump on their feet and they're going to tell -- say that Mr. Scott is misrepresenting the report. All right? Unfortunately, if we had more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I'm working on very tight time conditions here. If the Chamber would like to give me more time so that we can help the witness find each separate page, then I'm happy to live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think there is no doubt that if the Prosecutor is referring to certain pages in material, so we are talking about details, some phrase, some sentence, the witness -- the expert witness is entitled to know to which text he is referring. When we are preparing the same thing, we are giving the references on Croatian text for the witness and on the English text for the other people present in the courtroom. I think that the Prosecutor should tell to witness, This is on page this and this of Croatian language, of your original text. And this was always done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can count on our Registrar, because obviously on the screen we have one page in English and one page in B/C/S. Mr. Scott, please, could you resume with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not quoting any particular language right now. I referred to the section of his report and to his general conclusions, and I think he must be familiar with what those conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, in that section of your report, you say -- you conclude that these various Bosnian-Serb declarations, and assemblies, and other things that they were doing throughout this time, in these paragraphs, were illegal, undermine the legitimate authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and destabilised Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just recounted part of my synthetic conclusions in your own words. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have. You're absolutely right, I have. I paraphrased your conclusions, just like Ms. Alaburic paraphrased some material to you the other day. And I've paraphrased them correctly, haven't I, sir? You conclude that various of these declarations, associations, assemblies, were declared -- were illegal; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a doubt, they were geared towards excluding that part which was under the supervision of the Serbs and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is indubitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 75, you say that: "Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BH SDS, that is, the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb party, established, quote, these are your words: " ... illegal communities and municipalities in some parts of BH." In paragraph 69 to 70, you say that the Bosnian Serbs: " ... adopted the unlawful decision to establish the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, it's your word, "illegal," and it's your word, "unlawful." All I'm asking you, sir: You say that in your report, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's just a fragment, and it's clear, for the Court to gain an insight into the actual state of affairs legally, we're dealing with representatives of the Serbs which they voted at the elections in 1990. However, they set up an illegal -- apart from this assembly of representatives, and I said it was a paradox that the president of that assembly was the same person for the joint assembly and the illegal assembly. But that just illustrates what the situation was like in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so it's inconceivable from the aspects of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly. And, in fact, sir, in your report, you make reference to these entities being illegal, and I'd like to show -- direct your attention, please, to P10985, P10985. It will be in the third binder.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Can somebody help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure. Sorry, sir, we'll assist you. Binder number 3, 10985. Sir, this is a decision by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated -- the decision, itself, dated 1 November 1991, 1 November of 1991, published in the "Official Gazette" on the 28th of November, 1991, and this is one of the decisions, sir, is it not, where the Constitutional Court declared various of these Serb -- Bosnian Serb associations, assemblies, unconstitutional and illegal; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the decision, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just for example, decision Roman numeral I, immediately at the top: "To hereby annul the following: The agreement of association in the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina number ...," et cetera, and it goes on to talk about some other materials as well. But you agree with these results, right, and this is consistent with your analysis that we looked at a moment ago in which you say in your report that various of these associations and declarations were illegal and unconstitutional; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and I said with what intention in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you discussed on Monday, sir, some questions. One of them came from the President, Judge Antonetti. You discussed the question then, and I put it in this context of what you've said about the Serb organisations, it was put to you whether Herceg-Bosna was, indeed, also not a state or might be considered by some a state within a state, and you said -- and you testified on Monday, and this is at pages 44754 to page 55, 44754 to 55: "When we speak about the state politicological, and in terms of political science, sociologically, and I also think in legal terms, it is quite clear what it means, a state. It means that there has to be sovereignty. It means that no higher power is recognised in terms of sovereignty." And, sir -- so you're saying that that was why -- at least one reason why you did not consider -- or at least you argue that Herceg-Bosna could not be considered a state because it did not have this sense of sovereignty and no higher power, but you didn't explain at the time, and I'm asking you now, who then, or what then, was the higher sovereign power to which Herceg-Bosna owed its allegiance? If there was a higher power and it was the existence of that higher power that prevents it, in your analysis, from being a state, what higher power was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, you're wasting your time, because I said that clearly to the President of this Trial Chamber. We even saw photocopies of the documents. And in all the documents relating to Herceg-Bosna, as the supreme authority, is Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was explicitly written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, so that's your position. I want to be clear about that. So in that case, then, for example, the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the legal authority and legitimacy to remove Mate Boban from power? Mr. Boban, you're no longer wanted, you're subject to our control, we're sovereign, you're not; you're out of here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends how it was regulated under the law with regard to subsidiarity, who can replace some lower authority. There's clear procedure on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you just told us -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me, you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The time is limited. You just said -- the analysis is very basic. You just said what prevents Herceg-Bosna from being a state was because it didn't have sovereignty and that somebody else had sovereignty, and you just told this Court again that it was the Bosnian government -- the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had sovereignty. Now, you can't be almost sovereign or part sovereign or a little bit sovereign, and if they were sovereign, then they could have picked up the telephone, called Mate Boban, and said, Mate, you're out of here; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You live in a civilised world and you know that the president of the Government of France, or Britain, or wherever, can't just pick up the phone and tell the mayor of London, You're no longer the mayor, or something like that. So I think you at least, who live in well-ordered systems, can understand that, although in Croatian history what often happened, and indeed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was, indeed, how things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at it from the military side. Based on sovereignty, then, the commanders of the army of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was only one state that was nationally recognised as the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government of that state then should have been able to call up the head of the HVO, whether it be Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak, and give orders, say, We are the sovereign government, Mr. Jurcevic says we're sovereign, and, by gosh, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Praljak, you're dismissed. Now, is that what you consider sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my expert report, I quote a series of original documents also signed by the highest authorities, different types of the highest authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which undoubtedly confirms that the HVO was a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if need be, we can go through those documents, where this is written explicitly, Your Honours. To save me looking for them now, you can find it in my expert report, not to waste the Prosecutor's time. So as I say, there were a number of documents from 1992 onwards signed by the highest authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina that explicitly say that including the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the most important document -- which is the most important document as far as relations between the republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina are concerned, from May -- from July 1992 up until the Washington Agreements at the beginning of March 1994. But there are other documents as well, and if need be, I can show them, but it's on your time. I can quote them verbatim, and I think that you're well acquainted with that, too. You're aware of them. If not, you'll find it in the expert report and can take a look.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly be asked to slow down in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. Sorry. The interpreters again and again are asking you to slow down and to -- and actually to stop after your questions and answers. Really, during the last 30 minutes, it was terrible. Please, do comply with this request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I do -- I apologise for interrupting. It's just that the -- when the answers go on, the time is being spent, it's very difficult, and I do apologise to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I'm -- sometimes the reason I'm trying to stop you, and I apologise if it seems discourteous to you, but I accept -- I may accept your point, or it may be irrelevant to the point I'm trying to make. All right, you've just made my point -- you've just made my point stronger, sir. You've just said that, in fact, there are documents saying that the HVO was part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That makes my point even stronger. If it was, then there was one sovereign, and that sovereign could issue orders to it; correct? And there, again, my scenario is if it's part of the armed forces of a recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if the supreme authorities of that state call up to Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic and said, You're removed, that's an exercise of sovereignty, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are making things sound banal. I'm an expert here. I understand your time pressure, and you are putting me under pressure, and that makes me speak faster and I'm unable to elaborate things as a scientist. I have to say "yes" or "no", like a layperson, and you're using syllogisms. I know what the syllogism is. It's an example of making false judgements and false premises, and I can give you some examples just so that you can see how paradoxical that all is. So I studied philosophy, so I am aware of all that. So I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to protect me. I am an expert witness, and I'm being asked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have witness protection programmes, but that is not the case here. Please try succinctly to answer without always giving us background and referring to your scientific knowledge and merits and all that. We have your CV. Just stick -- read it to the frame of the question. It is for the Court to decide what your answer is worth in connection with a question, to assess what meaning it is to be given, but we -- unfortunately, it is an unpleasant situation. And on a human level and as another scientist, I can fully sympathise with the unpleasant feelings you have, the need to explain. I know that from my own person. But here, unfortunately, the situation is different. You are, to some extent, an instrument of the proceedings, and I would invite you to accept this role even if it is unpleasant and unsatisfactory. Please, Mr. Scott, continue. Now Mr. Scott has the floor. We cannot argue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to ask the question to you one more -- I've asked it now at least twice, if not three times. But because of -- given Judge Trechsel's additional guidance to you and so that it isn't said that you didn't have a further chance to -- opportunity to answer: Sir, you've told us that, in your view, Herceg-Bosna was subject to -- it wasn't a state because it didn't have sovereignty; it was subject to the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I've given you several examples of how that would work in reality. The last one I gave to you was on the military side, and I said if, in fact, the HVO was part of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if the ultimate authorities of that state issued orders to its commanders, including perhaps Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic, that would be an act of sovereignty, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In purely legalist terms, yes, of course, and that's undoubted. But as a scientist and historian, I have to take into account the circumstances that Bosnia and Herzegovina faced at the time, in particular its central government and its bodies that were unable to control even the BH Army, where they appointed the commanders and replaced them as they saw fit. And I speak about that, and everything I say is well-founded in my expert report. And I understand your need to use my expert report for your purposes, but I have to say what I think objectively, regardless of what you or the Defence need. And I gave the same response to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ask you not to give, sir. You answered my question. Sir, you considered it very important, and you say on page 79 of your report, and you mentioned this just a few moments ago: "It is very important to emphasise that the institutional signature block in all formal decisions, decree laws, and documents adopted by the highest bodies of the HZ-HB, first gave the name 'Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina'." Now, sir, isn't it true that Serb documents, documents from the Serb entities, the Serb associations, the Serb assemblies, did the same thing, the ones that you say were illegal?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection to this question because of lack of precision. Could his friend -- could Mr. Scott say -- could Mr. Scott say whether this pertains to 1991 or the time when Republika Srpska was created and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- the historical time, when he's talking about when these entities were established and were being operated. But, again, with a little patience, we might get to the next exhibit which will be exactly one of the documents that says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, would you look, please, at P11051, P11051, in the third -- at the end of -- the back of the third binder. It should be quite easy to find. Sir, this is the minutes of a joint Session of the National Security Council and the Government of the Serbian "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on the 14th of May, 1992. Would you also look at P11053. Go down two exhibits, please, in your binder. P11053.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we can just clarify about this document 11051, because we have another document under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the one that's on the ELMO, which I have -- it's the same one I'm looking at, 11051, minutes of a joint Session of the National Security Council in the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, that's what's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the Law on Ministries under that same number. The number is 11053, and that -- that's the minutes and that's the one we see here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, wait a minute, wait a minute. Before this gets any more complicated -- hold on. Witness, hold on. Let's just get it straightened out here. The wrong number may have been put on the document. Sorry, my apologies. There should be three documents together. One of the numbers may have gotten -- two of the numbers may have gotten on the wrong document. If you go to 11051, which I think has been corrected, I hope -- can we see what the Registry has as 11051 and see if we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jurcevic, the last three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the "Official Gazette," that's 11051, and 11053, that's the minutes from the Joint Session of the Council for National Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The three documents are all there together in sequence, 51, 52 and 53. Unfortunately, on my -- I may have gotten the numbers wrong. My fault, my mistake. I'm sorry. If you have 11051 in front of you, on that document, sir, doesn't that say: "The Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Monday, 13th June, 1992. "Pursuant to Articles 70 and 81, paragraph 2 of the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Article 5 of the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you go, please, to Exhibit 11052, which is perhaps the one that I -- if we can rely -- I'll rely --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've gone --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, if the Registry can show me what they've marked at 11052, I'll rely on that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the minutes of a meeting on the 6th of August, 1992. The title is "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and it refers to the 24th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and what you say is entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you'd look at the last document, sir, which is 1153 -- excuse me, 11053, this is again another set of minutes, and it's where I initially went wrong. Sorry about that. These are the minutes of a joint session of the National Security Council and the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that the fact that all these documents refer to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the fact that that's simply on these documents, doesn't change your view that these various Serb declarations or Serb assemblies were illegal or unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the Trial Chamber allows me to do that, this is a typical example. I am astonished by the ignorance of the Prosecution, and if I may, I'd like to explain why. What you call "Bosnia-Herzegovina," it says clearly "the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which was later called Republika Srpska, so this is the exact opposite. There is no Bosnia -- there's no Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state here. I think that this shows an elementary level of ignorance. I'm quite shocked, I have to say. But out of those three examples, if you allow me, Your Honours, and please do not count that as the Prosecution time because I don't want to prejudice them, you can see how superficial the approach is to this case on the part of the Prosecution. This document confirms that what is called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It will be for the Chamber to assess this. You have made your point, and I think it's not necessary to go on further. It's quite clear, what you've said. Mr. Scott. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case that when this is all said and done, and without looking at whether a particular phrase is written at the top of some documents or not, the totality of the evidence, the evidence you say you're aware of as a scientist, Herceg-Bosna was a complete political platform, it was for Croats and not Muslims, with its own government and its own territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think this is much too important. So in this document, which is called the "Official Gazette," there is no reference to any of the documents of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, unlike all of the documents of Herceg-Bosna. I don't want to prejudge matters, but these are notorious facts, and it's so banal, so trivial, that there is no need to explain it. In those three documents that we have just been shown, I would say this is written evidence, based on the official documents, that the Republika Srpska, which used to be called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, well, it is undoubted, even if you look at it very superficially, this is a reference to the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was occupied by the Serbian forces, and this can be used to prove the intentions of the Serb aggressor to carve out a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a separate state which would then be annexed to the Republic of Serbia. Each of these documents confirm that. And I would like to draw your attention, Your Honours, to the "Official Gazette," so the official journal of this state, in inverted commas, in the preamble, which is very important, in legal terms. I think they invoke some legal provisions, but none of those legal provisions are legal provisions of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is internationally recognised. They invoke their own provisions. So I think that here this is a serious mistake done by the Prosecution, and they are party to the proceedings. I think that they have just really caused a great deal of damage to their case. I have to say my opinion. I'm not here to speak in anyone's favour, but this is really astonishing. This is key evidence proving the exact opposite of what the Prosecution is trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the Prosecutor, through his questions, seems to, because I'm not 100 per cent certain, equate Herceg-Bosna with the Republika Srpska. This is what I understood through his questions. He stated that a constitutional court had declared the Republika Srpska illegal, so the same would apply to what is called the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I'm looking at the document now, P11051, and as far as the preamble is concerned, I can see that a constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is referred to. This constitution seems to have been adopted. The document we have before us is the implementation of this constitution. I haven't had time to check this yet. We have received that at the last minute. As far as you know, had the Republika Srpska drafted a constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what you've just said, the situation down there was very weird, and even the situation that we have in Bosnia and Herzegovina now, it's unprecedented. And this is the genesis of that situation, because there is no invocation of the constitution of the internationally-recognised state called the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the state that is internationally recognised is called the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. No. Here they invoke the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was later on formally renamed the Republika Srpska. So they're invoking the constitution of the part that seceded, I would say, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the political goal of those institutions, publicly stated as such. So the Serbian institutions systematically and persistently, in all their public documents of political and other nature, stressed that they did not want to be part of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this testifies to that. It is one of the number of public documents testifying to that, and it is undoubted. Here, there is not a single word invoking the common state, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it seems to me -- well, I don't doubt the level of knowledge of the Prosecution, but the situation down there, it is so incomprehensible in every way to the people who live there, who were born in well-organised states -- of course, no state is perfect, but Western states are so well organised that you probably find this incomprehensible. But this really is, I would say, a key document that helps you understand this whole story that we are trying to tell here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's why I put the question to you. If I have understood correctly, you are telling us that the Republika Srpska is one thing, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna is another thing, and you can't compare the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honours. And I explained that yesterday when I answered questions about the concept of the three constituent peoples. I said that two peoples, the Muslim Bosniak people and the Croatian people, and when I said "the people," I meant their structures, the structures that represented them and that were elected in 1990 at the elections, that the Muslims, to make things simpler, and Croats shared the same concept, at least in principle; keeping the state and internationally-recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina together. And the Serbian structure in BH had a completely opposite intent, in the public, in the media, politically, and legally. And we can see these are very important legal acts; and their concepts were opposite. They want the to secede. They wanted their "part," in inverted commas, to secede from the internationally-recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think there is a key difference there. And we can look at lower levels and see the nuances, the conflicts of interests and other problems. That's the key topic of my expert report, and it stems from a number of documents. But I'm happy that now the circumstances have led us to this point where we can show to the Trial Chamber some facts that you will have to deliberate on. But from a historiographical point of view, they are undoubted, as is my expert report, because it was done in accordance with the standards, not to satisfy the needs of the Defence or any other interests, but I wanted to do a paper, a scholarly work, that would be -- that would be founded in scientific terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, please try and slow down. In the evidence that has been adduced, I have realised, and anyone can realise this, that in the government of Mr. Prlic there was no minister of foreign affairs. Look at Article 6 of the document we have before us, P11051. Look at Article 6. There is a list of the ministries, and before item 4 there is a Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In point 4, point 4 of Article 6, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. But, Your Honour, almost all the documents from Republika Srpska, well, they didn't keep their intentions secret, they didn't hide their intentions at all. And I think that if you take up any newspaper or official gazettes of this kind, they had a very clear-cut concept, because they believed that they had such military might that they could implement it and that would then be verified by the international community. Unfortunately, Dayton did and left behind a creation which is a time bomb and a threat to security in South-East Europe -- North-East Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, if we understand this correctly, you are saying that the Republika Srpska was one thing and the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was another thing, and you can't compare the two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're trying to understand. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, based on what you've said in the last few minutes, one of the differences, then, is -- what you're saying is the Bosnian Serbs, they were just more obvious about it; correct? They were more open about their true intentions; is that what you say the critical difference was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, then --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You answered my question. The pending question, before the President intervened, was: Isn't it a fact, sir, that Herceg-Bosna was a complete political programme, it was for Croats, not Muslims, with its own government and territory? And I believe you answered to the effect, No; but I simply want to come back -- bring us back to where we were. Your answer to that question is, No; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, and I explain that in my expert report at length, and the ethnic structure -- I use the ethnic structure in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your answer is no. Sir, I didn't ask you for an explanation. I said is your answer, no? All right, please. If the Chamber would please have some assistance. My time is very limited, and I would appreciate some assistance from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the Prosecutor has a time credit, as the Praljak Defence team had. The Prosecutor needs to use his time as best as possible. He puts his question to you, you answer by saying "yes" or "no." If he would like to elicit a further explanation from you, he will ask you. Just provide your answer in a straightforward manner, even if, intellectually speaking, you are not satisfied; never mind. Just answer by saying "no," and if you say "no," that means your view is quite the opposite of his, and if he would like any further explanation, he will ask you to provide it. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can turn to Exhibit P00531, which would be in the second binder. And perhaps if the Usher can make this go as quickly as possible. P00531 in the second binder? Sir, this is a record of a meeting on the 30th of September, 1992, involving Dario Kordic and others, in connection with the Kakanj HVO. If I can direct your attention -- the courtroom's attention. Fortunately, there are some reference points. You have the title "Agenda," and then you have item 1, and then you have item 2. Do you see item 2, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under item 2, you first have an intervention or something said by Mr. Pejcinovic, then Dario Kordic, then Mr. Cabric, then Dario Kordic again. And about two-thirds of the way through that intervention -- well, depending on your point of reference, but if you go down through Mr. Kordic's intervention, probably -- well, again, I don't know if the lines would be the same, but probably 15 or 20 lines, but you'll find this section: Dario Kordic says: "You cannot impose an option through conflict because the Croatian people, not the Muslim people, are part of the HZ Herceg-Bosna. The civil authorities have been established. The HVO is the government of HZ Herceg-Bosna. We have people who inspire trust, like Jadranko Prlic, but it is impossible to expect that the government of Herceg-Bosna will solve everything politically within a single month. The negotiations on the future organisations of Herceg-Bosna are going slowly, as you've seen. What we are doing with the HZ Herceg-Bosna is the realisation of a complete political platform." Now, sir, that's a statement by Dario Kordic, the same man -- the same man -- the convicted war criminal that you visited in prison just several weeks ago, that you said was an important symbol. That's how he describes it, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have extracted a fragment, but I wasn't able to follow because I wasn't able to find it. And I'd like to look at the entire document first, but I'd like to stress that it is a document for the HVO area of Kakanj, a very small area, and in my expert report, I didn't enter into -- I didn't go into these low levels of municipal authority and analyse that. But if you want to waste your valuable time going down to this level, we can discuss that too. So what do you want me to testify about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Please, sir. We don't need that -- excuse me, sir. There is no real point in insulting me, unhappy as it may be.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me read it to you again. If the Chamber will allow me some flexibility on time, since I have to re-read the question again. Sir, I took you very carefully -- I took you very carefully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, put your question again. This time will not be taken off your time. Let me remind you, however, that you have three minutes left. You may put the question again, but this will not be deducted from your time, because he seemingly hasn't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I will ask the Chamber -- I thought I'd be finished in this first section, but I am going to ask the Chamber if I can, please, have an additional 15 minutes to finish my few remaining questions after this one. But the Chamber can consider that, but since we're paused, I thought I'll ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, please, I took the time -- I took my time to go very carefully through the document and find the interventions by Mr. Kordic. If you go down those interventions, you will find a section that says: "You cannot impose an option." Now, let me know when you find that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, are you talking to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me where the text is so that I can follow, please. This isn't deducted from your time, as His Honour just said. I'm on the document, but I don't know what part you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I tried to assist you, sir. I asked you a moment ago. Do you see item 2?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see item 2 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see the intervention by Anto Pejcinovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Anto Pejcinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see the intervention, the first intervention by Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see the intervention by Mr. Cabric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see the intervention by Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on the following page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look down through that intervention, through the series of lines, until you get to the point --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part? It's a long portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Scan down it, sir. Scan down it some lines until you find the place where it says: "You cannot impose an option."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph. I found it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read it to you again: "You cannot impose an option through conflict because the Croatian people, not the Muslim people, are part of HZ-HB, Herceg-Bosna. The civil authorities have been established. The HVO is the government of HZ Herceg-Bosna. We have people who inspire trust, like Jadranko Prlic, but it is impossible to expect that the government of Herceg-Bosna will solve everything politically within a single month. The negotiations on the future organisation of Herceg-Bosna are going slowly, as you have seen. What we are doing with HZ Herceg-Bosna is the realisation of a complete political platform." That's what Dario Kordic -- that's how he described Herceg-Bosna to a group -- to an assembled group of the HVO in Kakanj; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read this excerpt out correctly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's the truth of it, isn't it, sir? You know that to be the case, that what Mr. Kordic says here, in fact, is accurate, in the respects that I've put to you. It was a complete political programme, it had its government, it was the HVO, it wasn't for the Muslims, it was for the Croats, and that's the way it was, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, you have your interests, of course, but the excerpt that you read out begins with a very important sentence, at least as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. "You cannot change the options with conflicts." So that excerpt should be viewed within the context in which it was engendered. At the level of Kakanj municipality and in the legal sense, there's nothing compromising here, in my view, and ultimately of all these minutes, it's just one paragraph. And as far as the Court's concerned, I don't see that it's important if you generalise this on the basis of that, but here it says that you cannot impose an option, and he goes on to say how he views the situation in Herceg-Bosna, which is his right. However, documents like this, that speak for and against, exist in large numbers because, as I say, the level at which I did my studies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, has granted you this extra time, and you may run on until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 10.30? That wasn't exactly the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you talk also about the Croatian -- the Muslims arming themselves at various times, and you talk about, for example, the Patriotic League, and just one fundamental point. To the extent, sir, that the Croats had the right to arm themselves and organise themselves, I assume that you agree that the Muslims had at least an equal right to also arm and organise themselves, or was that, somehow, a right unique to Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At no point in my expert report, and if you have a different opinion, please substantiate it by quoting from my expert report -- anyway, at no -- at no point did I assess the right to something, and I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question is a "yes" or "no." It's very simple. Did they have the right or not? You don't need to quote your report. Just did the Muslims have the same rights to organise themselves and attempt to arm themselves, the same rights as the Croats claim to have had; yes or no? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all three constituent peoples had the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you devote a whole section of your report to the so-called Mujahedin, and I'm not condoning and I'm sure the Prosecution does not condone any crimes or misconduct by any groups on any side, but in concept, sir, this Chamber has heard all kinds of evidence about people coming from all over the world to fight for the HVO and the Croatian Diaspora, from Catholics and other parts of the world. Now, those are also foreign fighters, aren't they? Aren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign fighters existed in all parts of the former Yugoslavia. There were volunteers, there were mercenaries, who were not from the region, and in the HVO there was a unit of foreign volunteers, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There were no more -- apart from any misconduct that any of these groups on either side might have engaged in, there was no difference to say, Well, there were foreign fighters coming in to fight for the Muslims. There were foreign fighters coming in to fight for all sides, weren't there, including for the HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not to the extent to which --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The same as the funding of finances. We've heard again. We've had experts and witnesses come -- excuse me -- and tell us about the -- tell us about the fundraising from the Croatian Diaspora and how it supported Herceg-Bosna and how many millions of dollars and things came in. It was no different. The Muslims had just as much right to try to raise funds from whatever sources they could access as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I describe everything in my expert report, and I never questioned anybody's rights. And I write about that in detail in the different chapters for the BH Army, Muslim Bosniaks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm showing you one final document. Could you please turn to P10984 in the third binder, sir, P10984.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the document, dear sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'll look at the Croatian language version of it, sir. This is an announcement on the 10th of August, 1992, about the murder of Mr. Blaz Kraljevic. It's an announcement by the Party of Democratic Action in Croatia, SDAH, as it's explained here: "We condemn the murder of Mr. Blaz Kraljevic, commander of the HOS/Main Staff and his associates. It is known that Mr. Blaz Kraljevic publicly expressed his attitude towards the legal government institutions in Sarajevo. His statement that he recognised the legal government in Sarajevo and not the government in Grude and that his supreme commander was Alija Izetbegovic and not Mate Boban, portrays in a certain manner the dimensions and the causes of the conflict between the HOS and the HVO." Now, all of that that I've just read to you, that is a true and accurate statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a letter from the Party of Democratic Action of Croatia, and I wrote about that in my expert report, to the level to which this subject was elaborated. Now, this Blaz Kraljevic and some other killings, ideologically --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the content [Overlapping speakers] ... sir, the content is correct; right? You agree with it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I agree with the fact that Blaz Kraljevic was killed under strange circumstances, just like Ante -- a Croat, too, and that it was a certain political settling of accounts involved. However, it has yet not been established what the circumstances were, and there are ongoing trials, trials that haven't been completed; so, unfortunately, and not linked to this Trial Chamber, I'd like to know the background to all this, I'd be interested in knowing that, but it says here there's a final political position being put forward here. This incident did occur, an ugly incident, but the circumstances of it have not been elucidated. And I'd be interested to know, as a scholar, myself. Kraljevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You keep referring to your report, and you just said a moment ago you discussed it in your report, so let's look exactly at what you do say. It's page 94 in the English version, if we can have it on the e-court, but it's in your section under -- you can find your section if you need to, sir. I'm going to read it word for word. And, again, if I get it wrong, I'm sure I'll be corrected. But if you look in --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just have a little patience, please, for me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor is going to read the section, then the expert is having the right to have his original text in front of him. So either he would be given exact coordinate of the Croatian pages or he should be given a reasonable time to find this page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Roman numeral II, sir, in your section, Roman numeral II in the report you wrote, section 5.3. "Croatian Defence Council who ran HVO." That's the heading.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just let me take a moment, Your Honour. I found it, dear sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you go down through a series of paragraphs, you will find one that says: "There were many but Muslim/Bosniak members in HOS units." And you scan down under that section, sir, until you find the paragraph that starts with: "There were many Muslim/Bosnian members in HOS units."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. I found it, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say, in your report, and I'd like the courtroom to compare this with what the document we've -- I just read to you a moment ago: "The commander of the HOS was Blaz Kraljevic, a Croat who had emigrated to Australia and returned as a volunteer. He supported the co-operation between the Croats and the Muslim/Bosniaks. In early August 1992, 'the government in Sarajevo appointed General Kraljevic a member of the BH Army Main Staff.' Due to the many differences between parts of the HVO and the HOS, Kraljevic was soon killed in an ambush near Mostar. At this point, an all-out armed conflict between the HOS and the HVO was avoided by an agreement signed on 23 August 1992 by Mate Boban and the chief of the Main Staff of the HOS (Ante Prkacin). After this, the HOS was completely disbanded when groups or individual members transferred to the HVO or the BH Army." Did I read your report correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read the excerpts completely correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, of course, you didn't put anything in your report that wasn't true, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct, completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your answers. If I at any time seemed discourteous to you, I apologise for that. Mr. President, thank you for the time allowed. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something? Thank you. Nothing personal, I didn't take anything personally, and I thank Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Kovacic for redirect, Professor, I have a couple of questions for you. The first question deals with forged documents. Yesterday, when you were answering a question put to you by Mr. Scott, you said that in the Blaskic case, a number of forged documents had been presented. I was listening to you and trying to understand what you meant. Overnight, I had to go and consult the motion for review filed by Ms. Carla Del Ponte with the Appeals Chamber, and also I had to study the Appeals judgement rejecting the motion of Ms. Del Ponte. I'm sure you'll remember that Colonel Blaskic was sentenced to 45 years in jail by the Trial Chamber, and in appeal, after being acquitted on several counts, he -- his sentence was reduced to nine years. After that, Ms. Del Ponte made a -- filed a motion for review for the Appeals judgement to be reviewed, because she was unsatisfied with the new sentence, and she mentioned six sub-grounds that made it possible to review the trial, and one of them was the question that had to do with the MUP report which, according to the Prosecutor at the time, had been forged. The Appeals Chamber received a 20-page version of the document, whereas the original version was 40 pages long. And Anto Nobilo, the counsel at the Appeals Chamber, presented a forged report, according to Ms. Del Ponte. At least that is what she developed in her submissions. As you know, the Appeals Chamber rejected the motion for review of its judgement. Now, I listened to you carefully, and I was wondering what you meant when you said yesterday that there had been some forged documents.
